She Built a Six-Figure Career Cuddling Strangers — And Says It Has Never Been Sexual

Havenfall Chronicles

She Built a Six-Figure Career Cuddling Strangers — And Says It Has Never Been Sexual

HAVENFALL — Most people would struggle to imagine turning a hug into a career.

For Marissa Vale, it became a six-figure business.

The Havenfall woman has spent the last several years building a career as a professional cuddler, offering strangers something she believes has become increasingly difficult to find: completely non-sexual human touch.

Her sessions are simple.

Clients arrive, discuss their boundaries, agree on what kinds of contact they are comfortable with, and then spend the session talking, sitting together, holding hands, hugging or cuddling.

There is one rule that Marissa says has never changed.

Nothing sexual.

"No matter who walks through that door, they're a client," she said. "I'm providing comfort and companionship. I'm not looking for a relationship."


From strange idea to serious business


When Marissa first discovered professional cuddling, she thought it sounded almost ridiculous.

Then she realized people were actually paying for it.

She began offering short sessions on the side before eventually turning it into her full-time career. As her client list grew, so did her prices, with longer appointments, repeat customers and private sessions eventually pushing her annual income into six figures.

Her clients range from people who live alone to professionals who spend most of their lives working and rarely experience physical affection.

Some simply want to talk while being held.

Others reportedly spend most of their appointments in silence.


"People think it's sexual"


According to Marissa, that is the biggest misconception surrounding her profession.

She says clients are screened beforehand and must agree to clear rules. Sexual touching, sexual activity and attempts to turn a session into something else can result in the appointment immediately ending.

Professional cuddling organizations similarly emphasize that sessions should remain platonic and that practitioners should establish boundaries before contact begins.

"People hear 'cuddling strangers' and immediately assume something sexual," Marissa said. "But that's actually the opposite of what I'm offering."

She says the entire point is that affection can exist without romance or sex.


A surprisingly emotional job


The money may have initially attracted attention, but Marissa says the emotional side of the work is what keeps her doing it.

Clients sometimes arrive nervous and barely speak during their first session.

Others reportedly talk for hours.

"Sometimes people don't need advice," she said. "They just want someone to sit beside them and make them feel like they're not completely alone."

Professional cuddlers interviewed elsewhere have described similar experiences, saying sessions can involve emotional vulnerability and conversations about loneliness, while strict boundaries remain essential.


Six figures, one unusual career


Marissa refuses to describe her work as dating, companionship or sex work.

To her, it is a service built around consensual physical affection.

And while Havenfall still has plenty of people who find the profession strange, her bank account has made the argument somewhat difficult to dismiss.

She has turned something most people give away for free into a career worth six figures.

But according to Marissa, the most valuable thing she provides isn't actually the cuddling.

It's the feeling that, for one hour, somebody isn't alone.

— Havenfall Chronicle
